sources.quote: Judge Rodney Gilstrap Sets an Unwanted Record: Most Cases With Financial Conflicts
sources.searcher_note: Original WSJ story in its 'Hidden Interests' series; fetch blocked, headline only. URL slug rebuilt from a truncated link on a Temple Law repost; ID 11632920541 is from that link.

sources.quote: The Wall Street Journal found 138 cases assigned to him involving companies in which he or his wife held an interest.
sources.searcher_note: Summary of the WSJ finding: Gilstrap had the most conflicted cases of any federal judge, 138. Counts cover him or his wife, not a company list matching ours.

sources.quote: Some corporate giants were in the judge’s docket and in his portfolio, the Journal found, including Microsoft Corp., in which he made 53 rulings
sources.searcher_note: Rewrite of the WSJ story giving the per-company split: Microsoft 53, Walmart 36, Target 25. No Apple or AT&T numbers found in any source. Copy of WSJ, counts once.

sources.quote: Gilstrap had stock that would have required recusal in four cases, while his wife had an interest in a trust that would have required Gilstrap’s recusal in 134 other cases, the notices said.
sources.searcher_note: Gilstrap's own court notices: only 4 of the 138 cases were his own stock; 134 were via his wife's trust. Also carries his view that little-action and trust cases didn't need recusal.

sources.quote: the most common reason for such recusals from such cases is that a judge or their spouse hold shares in a publicly-traded company that is party to the case.
sources.searcher_note: Later coverage: Gilstrap recused from ParTec v. Microsoft with no stated reason; author guesses Microsoft shares. Speculation, not a finding.

notes: WSJ 2021 is the main coverage: 138 conflicted cases since 2011 (disclosures through about 2018), Gilstrap first among 131 judges. Our lead says 183 cases for Apple, Microsoft, AT&T, Walmart over 2010-20; the company set differs from WSJ's (Microsoft, Walmart, Target, IBM, Disney) and no source found mentions Apple or AT&T holdings for him. Gilstrap's notices split the 138 into 4 own-stock and 134 wife's-trust cases, which bears on 'while holding their stock'. Nothing found dated after 2026-06-30. WSJ page could not be fetched.
